extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, journalists, and policymakers interested in public opinion, propaganda, and media
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying conceptual criteria about how public opinion is formed, limited, and manipulated — including censorship, pseudo-environments, propaganda, media limits, and infrastructural channels. Useful for political scientists, journalists, and media analysts studying information flow and opinion formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-environment determines behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: What each man does is based not on direct and certain knowledge, but on pictures made by himself or given to him. 'The way in which the world is imagined determines at any particular moment what men will do.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: If an atlas says the world is flat a sailor will avoid the edge; if maps show a fountain of youth a Ponce de Leon will search for it. The pseudo-environment determines effort, feelings, and hopes, though not necessarily accomplishments or results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda as substitution of social patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda is the effort to alter the picture to which men respond, to substitute one social pattern for another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: formation of class-consciousness or national consciousness by organized effort; propaganda works by changing internal pictures rather than by formal argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between private opinions and Public Opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Those pictures which are acted upon by groups of people, or by individuals acting in the name of groups, are Public Opinion (capitalized); individual pictures inside heads are public opinions (lowercase).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic implication: study must distinguish individual internal images from the collective phenomena that affect policy or decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief external factors limiting access to facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief factors which limit people's access to the facts are the artificial censorships, the limitations of social contact, the comparatively meagre time available in each day for paying attention to public affairs, the distortion arising because events have to be compressed into very short messages, the difficulty of making a small vocabulary express a complicated world, and the fear of facing those facts which would seem to threaten the established routine of men's lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist when evaluating how accurately public beliefs map to reality; these constraints explain systematic gaps between events and public perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stored-up images, preconceptions, and stereotypes shape incoming messages
rubrics_metrics.description: Limited messages from outside, formed into a pattern of stereotypes, are identified with an individual's interests and in turn powerfully direct the play of attention and vision itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic note: incoming facts are not neutrally received; preconceptions fill them out and bias subsequent perception and attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crystallization: identification of stereotypes with felt interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes become identified with a person's own interests as he feels and conceives them; through this process private opinions are crystallized into Public Opinion, National Will, or Group Mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the formation of group-level opinion, trace how images become tied to perceived interests and thereby stabilized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative government requires expert representation of unseen facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative government cannot be worked successfully unless there is an independent, expert organization for making the unseen facts intelligible to those who have to make the decisions; personal representation must be supplemented by representation of the unseen facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: decision-making bodies need pre-processed, expert information about complex unseen realities rather than relying on aggregate lay opinion or the press alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press cannot be expected to substitute for organized facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspapers are regarded by democrats as a panacea for their own defects, whereas analysis of the nature of news and of the economic basis of journalism seems to show that the newspapers necessarily and inevitably reflect, and therefore, in greater or lesser measure, intensify, the defective organization of public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution: do not assume the press will produce sound public opinion for free; readers expect miracles at no cost, and the press's economic and news constraints shape what it can provide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and presentation of news shapes public perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups who control selection, framing, and distribution of news (e.g., military General Staff) can present only certain facts, and only in such a way as will be most likely to steady or direct the people; those words 'would paint a picture in men's minds of what was happening'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: wartime communiqués from Verdun were edited to steady public morale; selection, omission, repetition, and emphasis (e.g., casualty figures emphasizing enemy losses) produce intended inferences without formal argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda requires a barrier between public and event
rubrics_metrics.description: Without some form of censorship, propaganda in the strict sense of the word is impossible. In order to conduct a propaganda there must be some barrier between the public and the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military censorship is a clear example, but barriers can be legal, institutional, technological, or social; where direct access exists, organized persuasion is harder to impose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy and established secrecy create information barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Various domains of life are treated as private (e.g., salaries, directors' meetings, cabinet discussions); those barriers and varying standards of privacy limit what reaches the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological tip: when assessing an opinion, ask how the facts were obtained — who saw or heard, who was permitted to see, and through what channels — to judge distance between opinion and event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on circulation of ideas and the scale of effort needed to reach 'everybody'
rubrics_metrics.description: There are very distinct limits upon the circulation of ideas; reaching 'everybody' required enormous organized machinery in wartime (e.g., Creel's Division of News, Four Minute Men, posters, lantern slides), and such scale rarely exists in peace, leaving enclaves and ghettoes poorly informed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical implication: evaluate whether a communication effort had the resources, channels, and coordination necessary to produce a uniform public opinion; absence of such effort explains fragmentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural and infrastructural conditions affect information flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Travel and trade, the mails, the wires, radio, railroads, highways, ships, motor cars, and prospectively aeroplanes, along with tariffs, subsidies, and other political/economic conditions, influence the supply and quality of information and opinion in intricate ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing information spread, include material conditions (transport, communication costs, legal barriers) and recognize that infrastructural changes have mixed and sometimes adverse effects on public awareness (e.g., centralization of railways concentrating influence in capitals).
